p.x:
In my house, we try not to waste food. Every Sunday, my mum looks in the fridge. If it's almost empty, we go shopping. We only buy what we need.
If the bananas are too brown, my dad makes banana bread. If the bread is old, we feed it to the birds. My little brother doesn't like apples, so we cut them and put them in a box for his lunch with honey. Now he eats them!
When I'm full, I don't eat more. I put my food in the fridge for later. But my mum always says, "Smell it first! If it smells bad, don't eat it."

Every year, the average family throws away a lot of food. Here are some easy ways to waste less.
Plan before you shop. Check what's in your fridge and write a shopping list. Don't buy more than you need, even if there's a special offer.
Store food carefully. Put meat and fish in the freezer if you won't eat them soon. You can freeze bread, too, and simply heat it in the morning. Keep rice and beans in a jar so insects can't get in.
Look at dates, but use your senses too. The expiry date tells you when food may not be safe. However, many foods are still fine after this date if they look and smell OK. Stale bread can become toast, and old vegetables can go into soup. Of course, if fruit is rotten or covered in mould, throw it away.
Use leftovers. Reheat last night's dinner for lunch, or turn it into something new. Even fruit peel can be used: orange peel makes a lovely tea! And when you eat at a restaurant and can't finish your meal, ask for a doggy bag. Making a weekly meal plan helps too. Grandparents often know old ways to make perishable food last longer, such as how to pickle or ferment vegetables. Food with a long shelf life, like rice, is easy to store. Throwing food away is wasteful, especially when so many people face hunger. Some shops even give surplus food to charities, and 'best before' dates are about quality, not safety.

According to the United Nations, roughly a third of all food produced in the world is lost or wasted, while hundreds of millions of people suffer from malnutrition and, in some regions, famine. This contradiction makes food waste one of the most striking failures of the modern food system.
Waste occurs at every stage of the supply chain. In developing countries, much is lost before it reaches consumers, because of poor storage and transport. In wealthier countries, the problem is concentrated at the end of the chain. Retailers reject fruit and vegetables with minor blemishes or unusual shapes, and confusing labels lead shoppers to throw away food that is perfectly safe. In many countries, a sell-by date is intended for shop staff, not customers, yet many people treat it as a deadline for eating.
The environmental consequences are serious. When food rots in landfill, it produces methane, a greenhouse gas many times more powerful than carbon dioxide in the short term. If food waste were a country, it would be one of the world's largest emitters. Wasted food also represents wasted water, land and energy.
Solutions are emerging at every level. Some governments now require supermarkets to redistribute unsold food to charities instead of destroying it. Apps connect restaurants with customers who can buy surplus meals cheaply at the end of the day. Meanwhile, campaigns encourage households to adopt the thrifty habits of previous generations. Reducing waste, experts argue, is one of the simplest ways to improve global food security without producing a single extra calorie.
